newsitem.title: USA: Prudential strikes class-action deal with Florida.
newsitem.headline: Prudential strikes class-action deal with Florida.

text.p: Prudential Insurance Co of America on Thursday agreed to pay $15 million to the state of Florida and make restitution to an estimated 128,000 Floridian policy holders to settle state charges it cheated life-insurance customers.

State officials said at a news conference in Talahassee that they would drop opposition to a class-action settlement pending in a federal court in Newark, New Jersey, after the insurance company agreed to make changes in its proposed nationwide settlement covering an estimated 3.1 million people.
The class-action changes give most customers over 60 years of age full restitution and will guarantee complete restitution to those whose records had been destroyed, officials said.
A lawyer for the Florida Department of Insurance estimated that the average excess premium paid by affected customers was $2,300, though some had overpaid by as much as $7,000.

Officials gave no estimate of the size of restitution expected in Florida. But Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson said the company could pay as much as $1.5 billion nationwide to settle claims it had used deceptive sales methods known as "churning" to sell policies between 1982 and 1995.
The states of Texas and Massachusetts also agreed on Thursday to a settlement with Prudential.
Nelson said the Florida settlement would benefit policyholders across the country, not only those in the state, because Prudential has agreed to amend its class-action settlement.
"This is an amendment to the entire class-action settlement process, so it will help those across the country benefit from the changed class-action proposed settlement," Nelson said.

Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said the agreement reached late on Wednesday with Prudential Chairman Art Ryan called for the state to drop its racketeering charges against the insurer as long as Prudential lived up to deal.
The state had charged that Prudential executives acted to cover up the churning after Florida began its inquiry and ordered that key documents be destroyed.
Butterworth said Prudential executives had pledged to fulfill the terms of the agreement.
